system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Second-order logic
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Syntax and standard semantics with quantification over all relations and functions, expressive power (identity, transitive closure, finiteness, countability, PA2 categoricity), and metalogical failures (no sound and complete derivation system, non-compactness, failure of Löwenheim-Skolem). Excludes the cardinality and continuum hypothesis formulas.

ATOMS:
- CS-COMP-C09-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Second-order logic extends first-order logic by extending both the language and the definition of satisfaction to include free and bound function variables and predicate variables, together with quantification over them.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0192-s08] In second-order logic, both the language and the definition of satisfaction are extended to include free and bound function and predicate variables, and quantification over them.
- CS-COMP-C09-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: In the standard semantics of second-order logic, the second-order quantifiers range over all possible objects of the right type, namely all $n$-place functions from $|\mathfrak{M}|$ to $|\mathfrak{M}|$ for function variables and all $n$-place relations for predicate variables.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0193-s03] In the standard semantics, the second-order quantifiers range over all possible objects of the right type (n-place functions from |M| to |M| for function variables, n-place relations for predicate variables).
- CS-COMP-C09-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: In first-order logic, quantification is allowed only over elements of the domain, so only object variables may follow a quantifier, whereas second-order logic also permits quantification over function and predicate variables.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0192-s07] But, crucially, quantification is only allowed over elements of the domain, and so only object variables are allowed to follow a quantifier.
    [CS-COMP-p0192-s08] In second-order logic, both the language and the definition of satisfaction are extended to include free and bound function and predicate variables, and quantification over them.
- CS-COMP-C09-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: If a structure $\mathfrak{M}$ satisfies second-order Peano arithmetic PA$^2$ (the first eight axioms plus the single second-order induction axiom), then $|\mathfrak{M}| = \{\mathrm{Val}^{\mathfrak{M}}(\overline{n}) : n\in\mathbb{N}\}$, so a model of PA$^2$ contains no non-standard numbers.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0204-s05] PA2 consists of the first eight axioms above plus the (second-order) induction axiom:
    [CS-COMP-p0204-s08] A model of PA2 contains no non-standard numbers.
    [CS-COMP-p0204-s09] Theorem 8.19. If M ⊨PA2 then |M| = {ValM(n) : n ∈N}.
- CS-COMP-C09-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: In second-order logic, the transitive closure $R^*$ of a two-place relation $R$ is defined by $R^*(X)\equiv B_R(X)\wedge\forall Y\,(B_R(Y)\to\forall x\,\forall y\,(X(x,y)\to Y(x,y)))$, where $B_R(X)$ says that $X$ is a transitive relation including $R$, so that $\mathfrak{M},s\models R^*(X)$ iff $s(X)=R^*$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0201-s05] We can say in second-order logic that X is a transitive relation that includes R:
    [CS-COMP-p0201-s10] R∗(X ) ≡BR(X ) ∧∀Y (BR(Y ) →∀x ∀y (X (x,y) →Y (x,y))).
    [CS-COMP-p0201-s11] We have M,s ⊨R∗(X ) iff s (X ) = R∗.
- CS-COMP-C09-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: In second-order logic the sentence $\mathrm{Inf} \equiv \exists u\,(\forall x\,\forall y\,(u(x)=u(y)\rightarrow x=y)\wedge \exists y\,\forall x\,y\neq u(x))$, which asserts the existence of an injective function on the domain that is not surjective and uses no non-logical function symbol, is satisfied in a structure $\mathfrak{M}$ iff $|\mathfrak{M}|$ is infinite.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0202-s02] In secondorder logic, we can simply say that such a function exists.
    [CS-COMP-p0202-s03] This no-longer requires f , and we obtain the sentence in pure secondorder logic
    [CS-COMP-p0202-s04] Inf ≡∃u (∀x ∀y (u(x) = u(y) →x = y) ∧∃y ∀x y ≠u(x)).
    [CS-COMP-p0202-s05] M ⊨Inf iff |M| is infinite.
- CS-COMP-C09-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: There is no sound and complete derivation system for second-order logic.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0206-s07] Theorem 8.23. There is no sound and complete derivation system for second-order logic.
- CS-COMP-C09-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Compactness fails for second-order logic: there are sets of second-order sentences that are finitely satisfiable (every finite subset is satisfiable) but not satisfiable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0207-s08] Compactness is not true for second-order logic.
    [CS-COMP-p0207-s09] There are sets of second-order sentences that are finitely satisfiable but not satisfiable, and that entail some A without a finite subset entailing A.
- CS-COMP-C09-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: The Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem fails for second-order logic: there are second-order sentences that have infinite models but no countable models.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0208-s06] Theorem 8.25. The Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem fails for secondorder logic: There are sentences with infinite models but no countable models.
